summary:
FireAlert is a scientific web platform designed to harmonize NASA MODIS and VIIRS active-fire observations into a more consistent view of historical burning activity. The platform processes real satellite observations, accounts for differences in sensor resolution and observation timing, and uses spatial-temporal matching and statistical calibration to generate comparable activity measurements with uncertainty information.

FireAlert provides an interactive map, historical burning-activity calendar, sensor comparison, trend analysis, anomaly detection, and downloadable reports. Instead of simply combining hotspot counts, it preserves sensor-specific observations and clearly distinguishes measured data from harmonized estimates.

The project addresses the challenge by creating a transparent and reproducible framework for comparing observations from different satellite instruments across time. This is important because changes in satellite technology and detection capability can make raw hotspot counts difficult to interpret as real changes in fire activity. FireAlert aims to provide researchers, land managers, and emergency-response teams with a clearer and more reliable understanding of where and when burning activity occurs.
details:
FireAlert is a science-based web platform that combines NASA MODIS and VIIRS satellite fire data to create a more consistent view of burning activity over time.

What does it do or how does it work?

FireAlert collects historical active-fire observations from NASA datasets. It processes and organizes the data so that observations from MODIS and VIIRS can be compared more fairly. It uses common spatial and time references, matches nearby observations from the two sensors, and applies statistical methods to reduce differences caused by the sensors.

The platform also shows the original observations, matched and unmatched detections, uncertainty, sensor agreement, and validation results. Users can explore the information through an interactive map, burning activity calendar, scientific analysis, trends, and anomaly analysis.

What benefits does it have?

FireAlert makes it easier to understand historical fire activity using observations from different satellite sensors. Instead of treating MODIS and VIIRS data as completely separate datasets, it provides a more consistent way to compare them.

It can help researchers study long-term fire activity, land and forest managers understand changes in burning patterns, and emergency and environmental teams review historical fire conditions.

What is the intended impact of the project?

The main goal is to make NASA satellite fire data easier to compare and understand. FireAlert can support research and decision-making by providing a transparent view of burning activity along with information about uncertainty and data quality.

The approach can also be expanded to different regions and additional satellite fire products in the future.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software were used?

The project uses:

Frontend:
Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, shadcn/ui, MapLibre GL JS, and Recharts.

Backend:
Python, FastAPI, Pydantic, and SQLAlchemy.

Scientific processing:
NumPy, Pandas, GeoPandas, Shapely, Scikit-learn, and Statsmodels.

Database and storage:
PostgreSQL with PostGIS and Parquet for large datasets.

Data sources:
NASA FIRMS and NASA Earth observation datasets, including MODIS and VIIRS active-fire products.

How is your project creative?

The main creative idea is to focus on harmonizing satellite observations instead of building only another fire hotspot map.

MODIS and VIIRS have different sensor characteristics, resolutions, and observation patterns. FireAlert considers these differences and tries to make their historical observations more comparable.

The platform also makes sensor agreement, disagreement, uncertainty, and data quality visible to users instead of hiding these scientific limitations.

What factors did your team consider?

The project considers:

  • Differences between MODIS and VIIRS sensors
  • Different spatial and temporal resolutions
  • Data quality and observation coverage
  • Uncertainty in the harmonized results
  • Accurate spatial and temporal matching
  • Data source and processing version
  • Scientific validation
  • Reproducibility of the methodology
  • Clear separation between original observations and calculated results
  • A simple interface that researchers and other users can understand
  • Future expansion to more regions and satellite products
